environment.host: shared local Docker Desktop Linux/aarch64 VM

method.throughput: 8 concurrent persistent HTTP clients, 3s warmup, 15s/20s measurement; one record per request; shared-host rates vary and are not production capacity guarantees
method.delivery: Track unique IDs of every HTTP-200-acknowledged record; follow-up cases wait for zero queue size and up to 10s for downstream delivery; report unknown client transport-error outcomes separately
method.storage: Linux-local Docker volumes for completed normal/I/O tests; bounded tmpfs with a retained mount and filler file only for the completed ENOSPC fault. The full-size tmpfs tiny-capacity run was stopped before saturation and is incomplete.
method.retry: 100ms initial / 1s maximum backoff, expiry disabled to isolate storage losses; production retry settings are unchanged
method.scaled_tests: The completed 64-byte tiny-request cases use 4MiB queues and 8MiB/16MiB databases; full-size saturation was completed on disk with 16KiB payloads. Full-size 64-byte cases were stopped before saturation; no full-size tiny-request capacity guarantee is established.

conclusions: Disk queues are the chart default with fsync disabled, matching upstream; process-restart recovery passed, but this does not establish unclean-host durability.
Three full-size mixed-signal fill/drain cycles delivered all acknowledged records in both modes; disk completed nine compactions.
The 2x database budget rejected tiny requests before the byte queue filled and lost acknowledged records on storage exhaustion in two runs.
The 4x database budget held the same 37263 tiny requests as memory and delivered all acknowledged records in that tested workload.
Fsync adds throughput/latency cost; disabling it improved throughput in a repeat but does not fix storage-full failures.
Constrained disk I/O caused seconds of receiver latency and client timeouts despite mostly empty queues.
The ENOSPC fault recovered for new traffic after space was freed, but three of six initially acknowledged records were lost.

The full-size 128MiB disk queue / 512MiB database accepted 8163 requests with 16KiB payloads, rejected eight further requests with HTTP 503 at the logical queue limit, and delivered every acknowledged record without duplicates or storage-full errors.
Both SIGKILL and graceful SIGTERM recovery delivered all 750 acknowledged records with fsync disabled. Fsync-enabled SIGTERM recovery also passed.
The chart requires at least 4x the effective byte queue budget per database, including preset and queue overrides; this is a headroom guard rather than a universal loss-prevention guarantee.
